The CIA records describe a bright green circular object seen at Site 7 at Sary Shagan on one evening in late Summer 1973. The witness was a Soviet citizen, referred to as "Source." He had been watching a Canada versus USSR sport competition on television and stepped outside for some air. He saw what he called an "unidentified sharp (bright) green circular object or mass" in the sky, west of the site at an angle of sighting of about 70 degrees [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA].

The fuller account adds these observations [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA]:
- The altitude could not be determined, and Source could not estimate the object's diameter.
- A field comment says there were no clouds that evening, but Source believed the green mass was higher than cloud level.
- Within 10 to 15 seconds, the green circle widened, and shortly afterward several green concentric circles formed around the mass.
- Within minutes the coloring disappeared.
- There was no sound, such as an explosion, associated with the phenomenon.

The record lists the resolution as unresolved, and the agency or branch is not stated. It gives no explanation of what the object was, so it stays a description of an unidentified phenomenon.

The archive holds a second fragment with the same wording for the opening of the account. It covers the evening in late Summer 1973, the television sport competition, the green circular object, and the position west of Site 7 at about 70 degrees. It is a shorter excerpt and does not include the concentric circles or the lack of sound in its excerpt, though its summary mentions both [UNDATED-CIA-158652]. The archive files the two fragments under separate canonical events, from different source files (CIA-UAP-D001.pdf and CIA-UAP-011.pdf). I have not merged them, but the text closely matches, so they appear to describe the same reported observation.

The archive holds two records about the Tremonton, Utah sighting of 2 July 1952. Each is catalogued as its own canonical event from a different source file, so I am not treating them as a single merged event.

The first is [1952-USN-80203D], "Tremonton, Utah UFO Filming" (canonical event evt-0585, from DOW-UAP-D102.pdf). It says Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse filmed about 30 feet of 16mm color motion picture film. The location was seven miles north of Tremonton on U.S. Highway 30S, at 1110 MST. The film shows a group of 10-12 unidentified objects milling about in rough formation and proceeding westerly. One object reversed course and was tracked separately across the camera's field of view several times. The excerpt gives technical details: a hand-held Bell and Howell camera with a three-inch telephoto lens, and sixteen frames per second. Newhouse was driving from Washington, D.C., to Portland, Oregon, when his wife noticed objects in the sky that she could not identify. The resolution recorded on this fragment is "unresolved."

The second is [1952-DOW-141453], "Tremonton, Utah Pillow-Shaped Objects" (canonical event evt-0586, from DOW-UAP-D103.pdf). It matches the first record on witness, place, date, and time, and it also describes a group of objects milling about in rough formation, first noticed by Newhouse's wife. Its summary differs, however. It says two photographs were taken, and that the objects appeared too small on the film to show detail. Its recorded resolution is "identified," and the supplied text does not say what the objects were identified as or why. The agency is not stated.

The two records differ in medium (about 30 feet of motion picture film versus two photographs) and in recorded resolution (unresolved versus identified). The supplied evidence does not explain these differences or say how the two records relate. It also does not give an official analysis of the film itself.

The archive places the December 12, 1948 green fireball in New Mexico. The dated record, [1948-USAF-DDD5CA], gives the location as near Starvation Peak (Bernal, New Mexico) and Los Alamos, New Mexico. It describes the fireball as observed simultaneously from two stations there.

The coordinates in the excerpt put its appearance very nearly at latitude 35° 50′, longitude 106° 40′. It disappeared near latitude 35° 45′, longitude 107°. The record describes a nearly or exactly horizontal path of about 25 miles at roughly 8 to 10 miles altitude, and it is marked unresolved. The coordinates and the two named stations come from the same record, and the excerpt does not itself say which coordinates belong to which station.

Two other fragments mention a December 12 green fireball, but neither states a location. These are [UNDATED-DOE-80EBE8] and [UNDATED-DOE-BBFEBB], and both are undated and list the location as "not stated." I would not treat them as independent location evidence. The archive does not say whether they refer to the same fireball as [1948-USAF-DDD5CA].

The archive has one record about this, dated 19 November 1968 and located in the vicinity of Puerto Rico [1968-USN-6F2707]. It is a single fragment, and it makes up the whole canonical event (evt-0574), taken from the source file CIA-UAP-D023.pdf.

According to the summary, the USS Clyatt detected an unidentified object on radar. The object appeared for twenty-one seconds and closed on a fighter from the east to a distance of a few miles [1968-USN-6F2707]. The verbatim excerpt is badly garbled by the scan. It supports only the general outline: the Clyatt picked up something on its radar, the object showed for a short time, and it again closed on a fighter from the east to within a few miles. The excerpt is too degraded to confirm further details, such as the object's speed or the fighter's identity.

The record lists its resolution as unresolved. The evidence supplied gives no identification of the object, no official explanation, and no information on whether the fighter's crew saw anything visually.

The other Puerto Rico record in the results, the Fort Buchanan sighting of 8 April 1953, is a separate visual observation from a different year and has no connection to the Clyatt detection [1953-USA-F78A64].

The Colorado Springs 2022 narrative describes a potato-shaped object. According to the record, a former U.S. Army intelligence officer and four other members of his unit saw it over the Cheyenne Mountains as they left their office building [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

The verbatim excerpt says the object had distinct edges and appeared painted in a creamy or whitish opalescent color. The summary adds that it looked translucent and had articulating panels. It stayed still for about two minutes and then vanished. The witness described the disappearance as a cloaking effect, which is the witness's characterization and not an official finding.

The fragment is undated in the archive, though it is tied to the canonical event "Colorado Springs 2022" (evt-0424). The resolution recorded is unresolved, so the archive does not identify what the object was. This is the only fragment in that event.

The shape reported in the November 2021 sighting was a triangle, formed by lights. According to the record [UNDATED-FBI-380101], the witness first saw what appeared to be a singular light outside their back window at about 5am. The witness first thought someone was in the yard with a flashlight. After going outside, the witness saw the light split into two or three lights. These formed a triangular pattern with a light in the center, and the pattern remained for approximately ten minutes.

The summary says the lights disappeared after an accidental camera flash. The supplied excerpt does not include that part, so I am relying on the summary for it. The record shows the resolution as unresolved. The date is undated in the record, and the excerpt itself is partly garbled. The "November 2021" date comes from the title and the witness's statement of a first sighting on "11/§§/2021," with the day illegible.

The evidence describes a triangular arrangement of lights, not a solid triangular craft. It gives no official assessment of what the lights were.

A separate FBI fragment [UNDATED-FBI-A1566D] describes anomalous orb-like lights near a residence dating from November 2021. It is a different canonical event, and its supplied text does not mention a triangular pattern, so I have not treated it as part of this sighting.

The archive has two records on the 1946 ghost rocket reports, and they are separate canonical events from separate source files. The other records supplied are unrelated to Scandinavia.

The first is a general campaign summary, [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896], drawn from DOW-UAP-D099.pdf. It is undated in the archive, though the text places the reports from late May through October 1946. It describes "flying missiles" seen over southern Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway, characterized either as "a ball of fire with a tail" or as "shiny cigar-shaped objects." The excerpt says the press first reported them over southern Sweden in late May 1946 and gave them the name "Ghost Rockets." Reports followed over Finland and Denmark in June. By July, sightings over Sweden had greatly increased, and several had also been reported over Norway. The summary says Swedish authorities received nearly 1,000 reports. The fragment records its resolution as "identified," but the supplied text does not say what the objects were identified as, so I cannot say what that resolution means.

The second is [1946-NASA-A146CF], "Swedish ghost rockets," from a document titled "UFO's and Defense: What Should we Prepare For." It describes witnesses seeing generally fusiform objects, occasionally resembling spheres or disks, from February to December 1946. They flew most often horizontally in Swedish skies, in some cases leaving a luminous trail, and were also described as capable of very suddenly ascending or descending. The summary says the sightings caused concern among military authorities in multiple nations. This fragment is recorded as "unresolved."

The two records differ in some details. They give different time spans (late May to October versus February to December) and different descriptions (fireball with a tail or cigar-shaped versus fusiform, sometimes spherical or disk-shaped). The records also differ on resolution, with one marked "identified" and the other "unresolved." The evidence does not explain these differences or say which account is more accurate.

The supplied evidence gives no official explanation of the cause or origin of the ghost rockets, and it does not support any conclusion about their nature.

According to the archive record, a Crusader pilot on the night of 19 November (1968, vicinity of Puerto Rico) observed a UFO in full moonlight, with good weather and good visibility. The pilot identified it as a delta-shaped object about the size of a jet fighter [1968-USN-85858D]. The summary for this record also gives an estimated speed exceeding Mach 3. The excerpt I have is partly garbled OCR and does not itself show that speed figure, so I can only cite it from the summary. The record's resolution is "unresolved."

Some related records come from the same source file, CIA-UAP-D023.pdf, but they are separate events:

- On 19 November, the USS Clyatt picked up an unidentified object on radar that appeared for twenty-one seconds and closed on a fighter from the east to a few miles' distance [1968-USN-6F2707]. The evidence does not say this is the same episode as the Crusader pilot's visual sighting. It is listed as its own canonical event.
- On 24 November, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a high-speed, high-altitude target that pulled away rapidly from a different Crusader aircraft flying at Mach 0.99 at 45,000 feet [1968-USN-9E57C2]. This is a different date and a different event.

The evidence gives no official explanation for the 19 November Crusader sighting, and the records do not say what the object was.

The Baku case is [1955-CIA-E34C6D], "Triangular Object Launch Near Baku, Azerbaijan," dated 1955-10-04. It is a single fragment that forms its own canonical event, and the source is CIA-UAP-006.pdf. The record gives no agency or branch, and its resolution is recorded as unresolved.

Observation, as reported: A US tourist and three companions on a train saw a large triangular object on an airfield roughly two miles from the railroad. The location is given as between the train and the Caspian Sea coast, about 50-65 miles south of Baku. A large searchlight on the field illuminated the object, which the witness described as about the size of a US jet fighter, squat, and shaped like an equilateral triangle. It had three lights, one at each point, which the witness presumed to be two wing lights and a tail light.

The witness said the object was ejected from its launching site and made "not less than three and not more than seven" fast spirals (the text is OCR-garbled, but this is the apparent reading). It then climbed very steeply at about a 45-degree angle. The summary adds that the searchlight tracked it as it climbed.

The evidence includes no official assessment or explanation, and the record is marked unresolved. The identification of the lights as wing and tail lights is the witness's own presumption ("presumably"), not an established fact.

Other triangular-object records in the supplied evidence are separate cases and are not connected to Baku. One is [UNDATED-DEPARTMENT-3685C6], from 2023 in the Pacific Time Zone. The other is [UNDATED-NASA-ED673B], from Arizona in 1997.

The CIA material describes a single event: an unidentified object reported over Harare International Airport in Zimbabwe on 2 July 2008 [2008-CIA-052DE8]. It comes from the file CIA-UAP-017.pdf, and the record is marked unresolved.

Observation: The report says the object was hovering at high altitude over the airport in the afternoon of 2 July 2008. The excerpt says it was observed "possibly by both radar and optical means," so the detection method is hedged in the source and not firmly established. The summary describes it as disc-like, with rotating lights on its underside. It is said to have shifted colors and then quickly ascended out of visual range.

Limits of the evidence: The scan of the excerpt is badly garbled, so the archive's summary is more detailed than the readable text I can verify. The record does not state an agency or branch, and it gives no official explanation or assessment of what the object was. Nothing in it identifies the object's origin or nature.

The record for the January 30, 1949 Socorro green fireball is [1949-USAF-5C0132], a USAF fragment titled "Green Fireball of January 30, 1949," located in the Socorro neighborhood of New Mexico. It is part of canonical event evt-0403 and comes from the source file DOW-UAP-D017.pdf.

What it describes: a green fireball occurred on January 30, 1949 in the Socorro area. The record mainly concerns the follow-up. The verbatim excerpt says that, despite air and ground searches in early February along the "well determined earth-trace" of the fireball, no fragments were recovered. Its resolution is recorded as unresolved.

The fragment does not give a time, brightness, altitude, speed, or the identity of the observers. It says nothing about what the object was.

Two nearby records should not be confused with it. [1949-USAF-9D1046] describes a different green fireball over Socorro on July 24, 1949, at 8:26 p.m., and belongs to a separate canonical event (evt-0402). [UNDATED-DOE-5FC004] is an undated Department of Energy fragment that mentions a January 30 green fireball over Texas, with brightness comparable to the moon. The evidence does not tie it to the Socorro record, so I am not treating it as describing the same event.

The matching record is [2023-FBI-6A299C], titled "Black triangular UAP over Colorado Springs, October 2023." It is an FBI fragment dated 2023-10-01, with the resolution recorded as unresolved. It is the only fragment in its canonical event (evt-0582), and the event's primary narrative source is FBI-UAP-D030.pdf. The ICA-UAP-D001.pdf file is also linked to the event as an analysis of it.

Observation, as recorded: a witness saw a dark-gray cloud near Colorado Springs. The cloud dissipated as a large black triangular object emerged. The excerpt says the witness saw "a constant, diffuse red light on the bottom front point of a solid black triangular shaped object coming out of the cloud towards the south, southeast." As the object left the cloud it widened until the witness could see the whole equilateral triangle with a red light in each of the three corners.

The summary says the object first moved at about helicopter speed. It then accelerated to possibly Mach 1-2, made unusual banking maneuvers, and disappeared. The Mach 1-2 figure is hedged ("possibly") in the summary, so it should be read as an estimate, not a measured speed.

The evidence supplied contains no official assessment or explanation of the object. The record's status is simply "unresolved."

Other Colorado items in the results do not match this description:
- [UNDATED-LLE-2234ED] is a 27-second video transcript from a Colorado law enforcement officer in October 2023. It contains only indistinct background noise and no description of a triangle.
- [UNDATED-USA-599D8B] concerns a potato-shaped object over Cheyenne Mountain. It is undated and is linked to a Colorado Springs 2022 event.

The other October 2023 records here are set in the western United States and describe a fiery orb, kite-shaped objects, and vehicle-like lights. They are not the Colorado Springs black triangle.

The record for July 2, 1952 describes a seven-inch ball of flame with an eight-foot trail, sighted from 1717 North 1st Ave in Phoenix [1952-USAF-0585D4]. The report says it made no sound and showed no lights resembling known flying objects. It was in view for 3 to 4 minutes.

The archive summary gives the time as 0420 hours and describes an arc from northwest to southwest. The verbatim excerpt itself is garbled at the time entry ("@42@"), so the exact time rests on the archive's reading of the text. The excerpt does not include the direction of travel. The record's resolution is listed as unresolved, so no official explanation is given.

The supplied evidence identifies the source only as the file DOW-UAP-D102.pdf and does not label it as Blue Book material. This is a single canonical event with one fragment.

The other Phoenix records in the evidence concern different dates: a June 29, 1950 radar and aircraft pursuit [1950-USAF-B40F] and a July 7, 1947 disc photograph report [1947-USAF-C042].

The archive record for this is [1968-USN-9E57C2], dated 24 November 1968 and located in the vicinity of Puerto Rico. It comes from the source file CIA-UAP-D023.pdf and is a single fragment belonging to one canonical event (evt-0575). Its resolution is recorded as unresolved.

According to the record, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a "high-speed, high-altitude target." The target pulled away rapidly from a Crusader aircraft that was flying at Mach 0.99 at 45,000 feet. The excerpt is garbled by OCR, but it also says the range "again" held such a target, which suggests this was not the first such tracking. The record does not say what the target was, and it gives no specific speed, altitude, or identification for it beyond "high-speed, high-altitude."

A related but separate record, [1968-USN-85858D], describes a Crusader pilot's visual observation of a delta-shaped object on 19 November near Puerto Rico. It is a different event (evt-0576), and it should not be treated as part of the 24 November tracking.

The record is UNDATED-USAF-58C451, an undated USAF fragment titled "New Jersey radar-visual incident with T-33 chase." It places the event near Sandy Hook and Fort Monmouth, New Jersey.

What it describes: T-33 pilots chased a large disc-shaped object. The summary says that about 10 minutes later, multiple radar stations in the area began picking up signals, tracking at speeds up to 3,500 miles per hour. The verbatim excerpt is a speaker's informal recounting ("We had a real interesting one from, uh, New Jersey...") saying the pilots in a T-33 "chased something," and that all the radar stations in that area later began picking up "these objects going back and forth all over the skies." The excerpt itself doesn't give the disc shape or the 3,500 mph figure. Those come from the fragment's summary.

Some caveats. The record has no date, and it is a secondhand, conversational account, not a detailed report. The fragment lists its resolution as "identified," but the supplied evidence does not say what it was identified as or on what basis. It belongs to a single canonical event (evt-0592), and the source is DOW-UAP-D154.pdf.

A separate record, 1951-USA-EDD9, also involves Fort Monmouth radar. It describes radar sets tracking a fast, low-flying target on September 10, 1951, and is listed as unresolved. It is a different event with no T-33 in the supplied text, and the evidence does not link the two.

The archive evidence has two Sary Shagan fragments, and neither records an agency or branch. Both list "Agency or branch: not stated."

The first is [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA], "Green circular object at Sary Shagan, Summer 1973." It belongs to canonical event evt-0401, and its source file is CIA-UAP-D001.pdf. The second is [UNDATED-CIA-158652], "Green Circular Object at Sary Shagan Range." It belongs to a separate canonical event, evt-0441, and its source file is CIA-UAP-011.pdf.

The "CIA" in each case ID and source filename may suggest a CIA origin for the documents. The fragments themselves do not record an agency or branch, so I can't state one from the field. Both fragments record the resolution as unresolved.

The USS Clyatt radar case is dated 1968. The record, titled "USS Clyatt Radar Detection, 19 November," gives the date as 19 November 1968 and places it in the vicinity of Puerto Rico [1968-USN-6F2707]. The year comes from the archive's recorded date and canonical event label. The garbled verbatim excerpt only preserves "On 19 Novemh" and does not show the year in its legible text.

The record describes the USS Clyatt picking up an object on radar that appeared for twenty-one seconds and closed on a fighter from the east to a few miles' distance. Its recorded resolution is unresolved [1968-USN-6F2707].

The Tremonton filming fragment, "Tremonton, Utah UFO Filming" [1952-USN-80203D], records its agency or branch as USN. It describes Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse filming about 30 feet of 16mm color film of a group of objects near Tremonton on 2 July 1952, and the fragment's recorded resolution is "unresolved."

The archive also holds a separate fragment about the same date and place, "Tremonton, Utah Pillow-Shaped Objects" [1952-DOW-141453]. It has no branch stated, and it belongs to a different canonical event (evt-0586) from the filming fragment (evt-0585). So the branch answer applies only to the filming fragment, and the other Tremonton fragment does not record a branch.

The Phoenix ball-of-flame fragment, [1952-USAF-0585D4], records its resolution as "unresolved."

That fragment describes a seven-inch ball of flame with an eight-foot trail, sighted from Phoenix, Arizona on July 2, 1952. It was seen at about 0420 hours for roughly 3 to 4 minutes, and the record notes no sound or lights resembling known flying objects. The "unresolved" status means the fragment itself does not record an identification or explanation for the object. The supplied evidence does not include any further official assessment of it. It is a single fragment belonging to one canonical event, evt-0584, and its source is the file DOW-UAP-D102.pdf.

The Baku triangular-object fragment, [1955-CIA-E34C6D], records its location as "Between train and Caspian Sea coast, Azerbaijan SSR, approximately 50-65 miles south of Baku." The record is dated 1955-10-04 and is titled "Triangular Object Launch Near Baku, Azerbaijan."

The location is an approximate description of where the witnesses were, not a precise site. The fragment describes a US tourist and companions on a train who saw the object on an airfield about two miles from the railroad. The archive places this fragment in a single canonical event, evt-0414, which uses the same location text, and the source file is CIA-UAP-006.pdf. The agency or branch is not stated on the fragment.

The location text recorded for the Cheyenne Mountain observation is "Cheyenne Mountains" [UNDATED-USA-599D8B]. The fragment's location field uses the plural form, and the verbatim excerpt repeats it: the former Army intelligence officer and four unit members observed a UAP "over the Cheyenne Mountains" as they exited their office building.

The fragment gives no date and records its resolution as unresolved. It belongs to one canonical event, evt-0424, titled "Colorado Springs 2022." That title is the event label, not the location text on the fragment. The fragment's own location field does not mention Colorado Springs or a year.

The December 20, 1948 Los Alamos green fireball fragment, "Green Fireball of December 20, 1948," records the branch as USAF [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. It is the only fragment in its canonical event (evt-0406), and its resolution is recorded as unresolved.

Don't confuse it with the December 12, 1948 fragment, which is a separate canonical event near Starvation Peak and Los Alamos. That fragment also lists USAF as its branch [1948-USAF-DDD5CA].

The Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range high-speed target fragment is recorded with the date 1968-11-24 (24 November 1968) [1968-USN-9E57C2]. The text of the fragment itself only says "On 24 November" and does not state a year. The year 1968 comes from the archive's date field for the record and from its canonical event entry, which places the event in the vicinity of Puerto Rico in 1968. The fragment is unresolved, and it is the only fragment in that event.

The archive has two ghost-rockets fragments, and each records a different location.

The fragment titled "Ghost Rockets over Scandinavia - General Campaign" [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896] records the location as southern Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway. It belongs to canonical event evt-0579. Its excerpt says the flying missiles were first reported over southern Sweden in late May 1946, then over Finland and Denmark in June. Sightings over Sweden increased by July, and several were also reported over Norway. The fragment's recorded resolution is "identified." It is undated, though the text places the reports from late May through October 1946.

The fragment titled "Swedish ghost rockets" [1946-NASA-A146CF] records the location as "Swedish skies, Scandinavia." It is dated 1946-06-01 and belongs to a separate canonical event, evt-0338, from a different source. Its recorded resolution is "unresolved."

If you meant the first fragment, the answer is southern Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway. If you meant the second, it is Swedish skies, Scandinavia.

Yes. The October 2023 Colorado Springs triangular report, [2023-FBI-6A299C], has "FBI" recorded as its agency or branch in the fragment metadata. The fragment is titled "Black triangular UAP over Colorado Springs, October 2023" and is dated 2023-10-01.

Its primary narrative source is the file FBI-UAP-D030.pdf, which fits the FBI label. The event also has an analysis_of_event relationship with ICA-UAP-D001.pdf. The fragment belongs to canonical event evt-0582 and is the only fragment in it.

The fragment's summary and excerpt are a witness account: a dark-gray cloud dissipated, and a solid black equilateral triangle with a red light at each corner emerged. The resolution recorded on the fragment is "unresolved."

The archive describes the Western U.S. 2023 series (western-us-event-2023, "Western US Event") as 21 canonical events. It is a series of separate events grouped together, not a single event.

The count of member fragments is different from the count of events. The series lists 28 member case IDs, but those are fragments, and some of them belong to the same canonical event. For example, five fragments [UNDATED-FBI-FEDFE7], [UNDATED-FBI-4557DC], [UNDATED-FBI-2EAE94], [UNDATED-FBI-42FC0E], and [UNDATED-FBI-578E28] all fall under one canonical event, evt-0452. So the number of fragments should not be read as the number of events.

The evidence I was given shows only some of the 21 events:

- evt-0313 is the "Transparent Kite" observation [UNDATED-OTHER-E3736E].
- evt-0314 is the "Dark Kite" observation [UNDATED-OTHER-FC97CA].
- evt-0315 is the "Orbs Launching Orbs" account [UNDATED-OTHER-26A05E].
- evt-0422 is the second orange ball with a vertical red light pattern [UNDATED-FBI-CD3613].
- evt-0452 is the multi-fragment event described above.
- evt-0456 is the yellow light seen months later [UNDATED-FBI-C4AD20].

That is six of the 21 canonical events. The remaining events are not described in the supplied evidence, so I can't say more about them. The answer to your question is 21 events, counted as canonical events in the series.

The archive links the Colorado Springs 2022 event (evt-0424) to three source files. The event has one fragment, [UNDATED-USA-599D8B], titled "Cheyenne Mountain UAP observation by Army intelligence officer." The fragment is undated and its resolution is recorded as unresolved.
